body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Five camp talks for Cordelia, about how Cordelia feels about the party and about the road. The talks that depend on how the party treats Cordelia are not about any deed in particular. The companion is CORDELIA SKEIN (call them Cordelia in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these five talks, in this order, with these keys. Every talk is a private word at the fire in a different mood. Do not repeat a topic across them.

TALK strained. Cordelia has lost faith in the party: the party's choices have drifted away from what Cordelia holds dear (read the note's "Approval moments" for what they like and dislike). Do not claim a specific deed; speak of "the way things have gone" and name what Cordelia cares about. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row (where they sit: apart from the fire, what their hands are doing), then 3 or 4 SAY rows saying what is wrong, in their own voice, stern and hurt, not shouting. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (listens, owns it, asks them to say what would mend it); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies: 1 reply row each for the cold one, 2 rows for the good one.

TALK doubt. Cordelia is doubtful: not angry, but they have doubts about how the party goes about things. Gentler than strained, more puzzled and wary. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 answers well (takes the doubt seriously and asks what they would do differently); OPTION 2 answers coldly (a flip remark that brushes the doubt off); OPTION 3 says nothing (stays by the fire, no words; this reply has NO REASON row and is 1 NARRATOR row plus at most 1 SAY row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows for the other two, each with a REASON row.

TALK act1. The first night in Wickermoor, a few hours after the Ghostlight Express crashed. Cordelia is still shaken and in their own way trying to be useful. They talk about the crash, the Hollow, the endless night and the Crooked Moon through their own eyes (their trade, their habits, their fears from the note), not about plot. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (a second NARRATOR row is allowed). Three options: OPTION 1 asks how they are holding up; OPTION 2 shares something of the party's own; OPTION 3 says they should get some rest and leaves it there. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act2. Deep in the troubles of the Hollow: the party has been through a lot and Cordelia has seen the party fight, win and lose. Something small has shifted in how Cordelia sees these people. Keep to the Hollow in general: name no place and no event except the Crooked House (the haunted manor on the hill, already cleansed) and the crash. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles as act1. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK act3. The last stretch has begun; whatever is coming is close, and everyone knows it. Cordelia is weary, truthful and a little funny about it, and says something about what the road has made of them and the party. Name no place and no event except the Hollow in general. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options in the same three roles. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: strained, doubt, act1, act2, act3.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/cordelia_skein-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for CORDELIA SKEIN (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Cordelia likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/cordelia_skein-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Cordelia, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK strained
NARRATOR: Cordelia sits well back from the firelight on a damp root, her four lower hands wiping soot from her thorax vials with a linen rag.
SAY: I have been reviewing the trajectory of our recent decisions, and the methodology is frankly appalling.
SAY: When presented with rare anomalies, you reach for a heavy blunt instrument or offer me that dreadful, moist-eyed pity.
SAY: We are wasting priceless specimens on superstition and panic, and I did not leave the dark of Nerukhet to watch ignorance triumph.
SAY: If you intend to treat every pathology in this valley as a monster to be smashed or wept over, my expertise is entirely redundant.
OPTION 1: We have been careless. Tell us how to approach this properly.
OPTION 2: We do what keeps us alive, not what fills your notebooks.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: You could begin by holding the torch steady before you swing the axe, darling.
SAY: Bring me the next intact specimen we encounter, and let us see if your discipline improves under observation.
REASON: You heard my complaint and asked how to mend our methods.
REPLY 2
SAY: Survival without comprehension is merely the reflex of a lower organism, though I suppose it keeps the blood pumping.
REASON: You brushed off my work at the fire.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The logs settle in a shower of red sparks while Cordelia checks the brass seal on her pack in the quiet.
SAY: Silence is at least clean data, so I shall leave you to the smoke.
TALK doubt
NARRATOR: Cordelia stands near the edge of the camp, spinning a short strand of crimson silk between two fingers and watchin' it dissolve into mist.
SAY: Forgive the interruption, darling, I am merely trying to calibrate the logic behind the way things have gone lately.
SAY: You leave half our inquiries unfinished in the dirt, as though curiosity were a hazard rather than our sole advantage.
SAY: One begins to wonder whether you are conducting an expedition or simply stumbling from one loud noise to the next.
OPTION 1: Fair point. What are we missing when we move on so fast?
OPTION 2: Overthinking gets people killed out here.
OPTION 3: Say nothing and stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
SAY: Every aberration in this valley carries the signature of what altered it in the humours and the bone.
SAY: Give me five quiet minutes with a scalpel after the next scuffle, and I promise the ratio of answers to bruises will improve.
REASON: You took my doubts seriously and asked what I would change.
REPLY 2
SAY: How delightfully brisk, darling, I shall remember that philosophy when your humours require an urgent assay.
REASON: You laughed off my doubts about our pace.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Cordelia lets the last red thread vanish from her knuckles and folds her lower arms neat across her ribs.
SAY: We can resume the peer review when the morning mist clears, provided morning ever arrives.
TALK act1
NARRATOR: Cordelia perches on an upturned crate near the coals, six eyes wide under the leering crone's face of the Crooked Moon.
SAY: Fascinating pathology!
SAY: When the Ghostlight Express left the rails, the sudden deceleration nearly unseated the third ruby vial on my thorax.
SAY: Had the glass fractured against the upholstery, my somatic calibration would have soured before we crawled out of the wreckage.
SAY: Look at the sky above Wickermoor Hollow, darling, not a single solar clue to regulate the pineal humours.
SAY: Just that enormous, grinning moon hanging over the trees like a preservative lamp in an old lecture hall.
SAY: I have already catalogued three distinct fungal spores in the fog, and none of them belong to a waking meteorology.
SAY: Still, so long as my vials remain stoppered and the fire stays bright, I have no intention of slipping back into the dark.
OPTION 1: Your hands are steady now, but how are you holding up?
OPTION 2: None of us expected to walk away from a wreck like that.
OPTION 3: Put the vials away for tonight and get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She taps the glass plug over her sternum with a clean, sharp click of her claw.
SAY: My resting pulse is eleven beats above baseline, which is an entirely rational response to derailment.
SAY: Keep the lantern lit near my branch tonight, darling, and my cortex will settle by the third watch.
REASON: You asked how I was holding up after the crash.
REPLY 2
SAY: Statistically, our survival argues for either extraordinary bone density or an experiment that has not yet reached its second chapter.
SAY: I much prefer to be the one holding the pencil when the variables turn lethal.
REASON: You shared a quiet word with me about surviving the wreck.
REPLY 3
SAY: A prudent prescription, though I shall sleep with my upper eyes half-open until I trust this fog.
SAY: Do try not to roll into the embers, as burn salve takes three hours to distil properly.
REASON: You told me to pack my notes and get some rest.
TALK act2
NARRATOR: Cordelia warms a glass dropper between her upper palms while her lower hands mend a frayed strap on her leather pack.
SAY: Since we walked out of the Crooked House, I have been forced to revise several foundational hypotheses about this company.
SAY: Back in Nerukhet, any group subjected to that degree of ectoplasmic stress would have fractured into mutual vivisection by the second hour.
SAY: Yet here we sit in the Hollow, bruised and lightly scorched, passing the kettle as though haunts were merely inclement weather.
SAY: Do hold still, this will only tingle.
SAY: There, a tiny smear of soot on your sleeve that was obscuring my view of the weave.
SAY: I used to regard companions strictly as mobile control groups with regrettably thin skin.
SAY: It is mildly alarming to discover that I now factor your survival into my primary equations rather than the margin of error.
OPTION 1: How are you holding up after everything we have seen here?
OPTION 2: We have all grown used to watching each other's backs.
OPTION 3: Save the equations for tomorrow and get some rest.
REPLY 1
SAY: My humours are remarkably lucid, darling, though the air in this valley leaves an odd mineral taste on the tongue.
SAY: So long as there is a clean fire and a sharp mind beside me, the old caverns feel very far away.
REASON: You asked how I was faring deep in the Hollow.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Cordelia tilts her head, the firelight catchin' the six dark lenses of her eyes.
SAY: Mutual preservation is a sound evolutionary strategy, even if you insist on calling it friendship.
SAY: I shall endeavour to keep my acid splashes well clear of your boots on the next road.
REASON: You spoke of how the party looks out for one another.
REPLY 3
SAY: Even the most rigorous researcher must occasionally yield to cellular fatigue.
SAY: Wake me if the fog thickens, darling, or if anything with more than four legs approaches the perimeter.
REASON: You told me to set my work aside and rest.
TALK act3
NARRATOR: The fire burns low and blue at the edge of the dark, and Cordelia sits close to the heat with all eight limbs drawn in.
SAY: If you examine the state of my boots, darling, you will observe that Wickermoor Hollow has thoroughly eroded the polish.
SAY: We are nearing the final stage of the assay, and even the air smells like a condenser about to boil over.
SAY: When we first crawled out of the train, I was terrified that one cracked vial would send my mind straight back to the nursery dark.
SAY: Now my knuckles are barked, my ratios are written on the wind, and I have never thought more clearly in my life.
SAY: Whatever waits for us at the end of this valley, it is going to find us exceedingly difficult to digest.
SAY: I must confess, having three stubborn anomalies at my shoulder makes the prospect of a lethal conclusion almost invigorating.
OPTION 1: You sound tired beneath the lecture. How are you holding up?
OPTION 2: Whatever comes next, we will face it together.
OPTION 3: Rest while we still have the fire to ourselves.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She lets out a breath that mists in the chill and rests two lower hands flat on her knees.
SAY: Tired to the very marrow, darling, yet my hand has not shaken once since the moon rose.
SAY: It is a novel sensation to be exhausted by the road ahead rather than the past behind me.
REASON: You looked past my lecture to ask how I was holding up.
REPLY 2
SAY: Together is an imprecise metric, yet in your case the calibration has proven unimpeachable.
SAY: Let us make sure the final record shows we gave the dark a thorough examination before the end.
REASON: You promised we would face the end of the road together.
REPLY 3
SAY: A brief suspension of consciousness seems acceptable before the final trial.
SAY: Keep the coals banked, darling, I have grown rather fond of waking up to this untidy little camp.
REASON: You urged me to rest by the fire before the end.
